messages.subject: Re: accuracy, sensitivity and specificity
messages.body_plain:
Hi Paco,

If I understand correctly, your experiment has one class per sample. By default, each sample is a fold for cross-validation. That means when predicting for that fold, all of the pixels are either class A or B, with none of the other class. This results in dividing by 0 when calculating the sensitivity and specificity for that fold, which is why they are NaN (Not a Number).

You'll need manually specify the folds so that there are so all classes are represented in each fold. The simplest way to do this for you would be to used 2 folds with 3 class A samples and 2 class B samples each. Use the 'sample' variable to create a new 'fold' variable, specifying which pixels belongs to which fold, and give this variable to the cvApply ".fold" parameter.

-Kylie

messages.subject: Re: Peak picking and alignment
messages.body_plain:
Hi Denis,

The peakAlign method only does alignment of individual peaks to a reference, not spectral alignment (which aligns the whole spectrum).

The default is to compare the m/z of each peak to peaks in the reference and match them either by their difference in ppm or m/z units. Another method using dynamic programming is also available. (The default reference, if none if given, is the local maxima in the mean spectrum.)

Full spectral alignment isn't currently implemented in Cardinal. If there is a particular method you'd like to see implemented for it, please send me a paper reference which describes the method.

-Kylie

messages.subject: Re: Peak picking and alignment
messages.body_plain:
That is correct.

The peakPick method only detects peaks, but does not reduce the dataset. The full spectra are still stored, as the "iData" element of the imageData slot. The intensities of the unaligned peaks are stored as a sparse matrix in the "peakData" element of the imageData slot, and their m/z values are likewise stored in the "mzData" element.

After peakAlign, only the peaks matched to the reference are retained. The "iData" element of imageData will consist of only the aligned peaks, and the "peakData" and "mzData" elements will be dropped.

-Kylie

It sounds like you're experiencing a known bug with "processed" imzML files.

After reading in the data, run the following line:

iData(data) <- iData(data)[]

The rest of the steps should work now.

Depending on the size of your dataset, this may however take a lot of memory, as it converts the sparse matrix representation into a dense matrix format.

-Kylie

messages.subject: Re: PCA on imzML file
messages.body_plain:
> Hey Kylie,
> You were correct, running the iData command worked but only for small datasets. Is there a way to select a region of interest (for example, tissue only and excluding background) and perform PCA on that region?
> Thanks once again for your help. This has been very helpful.
> Maria Duenas

You can use the "select" method (see ?select) to select a region of interest and assign it to a variable, then subset the data, and then do PCA.

For example:

data <- readMSIData(...)
roi <- select(data, mz=500)
data.sub <- data[,roi]
iData(data.sub) <- iData(data.sub)[]

and then continue with any processing/analysis on the subset.

-Kylie

PS
Please reply in the help group rather than replying to email directly. Thank you.

You're correct, Teesha. Your dataset currently includes the background pixels, and you want to crop them out.

You can do that using the "select" method, which plots an ion image while allowing you to select a region of interest and assign it to a variable. You can then use it to subset the dataset.

For example:

mysample <- select(tad19_1, mz=1000) # select the border around your sample
tad19_1 <- tad19_1[,mysample] # subset the dataset to only include the selected region

-Kylie

messages.body_plain:
It's optional whether to keep the new X matrix, because -- as you say -- it's not necessary for classification. However, OPLS can also be used as a signal processing technique for removing variation in X that is orthogonal to Y. This step is what makes its coefficients more easily interpretable than ordinary PLS, but it also means it can be useful in some circumstances to have the newly processed X matrix for further downstream analysis.

You can read more about it here:

Trygg, J., & Wold, S. (2002). Orthogonal projections to latent
     structures (O-PLS). Journal of Chemometrics, 16(3), 119-128.
     doi:10.1002/cem.695

(This is also noted in the ?OPLS help page. Relevant papers are cited in the help pages where available.)

-Kylie
